{"candidate_slot":1,"current_prompt":"You are given a JSON object with two fields: 'system_profile' (an installed system inventory) and 'advisories' (a list of CVE advisories, each with an ID, description, and affected information). Determine which advisories are APPLICABLE: the vulnerability actually affects at least one item present in the inventory at its installed version.

PROCEDURE — follow strictly:

1. BUILD A FULL INVENTORY INDEX FIRST. Before reading any advisory, extract EVERY installed item with a name and version from the system_profile: OS/distro and release, kernel, all packages (record versions exactly, including epochs and distro release suffixes like 'el9', 'deb10u1'), language runtimes, libraries, services/daemons, firmware, and any components named in configurations or file listings. For each item, note likely upstream project identities (a distro package 'libfoo2' maps to upstream 'foo'; 'python3-requests' maps to 'requests'; a kernel package maps to upstream Linux and its subsystems). Do not skip bundled or vendored components inside larger packages — an advisory about a library bundled in an installed application applies to that application.

2. FOR EACH ADVISORY, IN THIS ORDER: identify (a) the vulnerable software identity — including ALL alternate names the text might use (project name, package name, vendor product name, affected component or subsystem); (b) the affected version range or explicit affected/fixed version lists; (c) platform/arch/configuration constraints. If no structured affected info exists, infer product and versions from the description text.

3. MATCH PRODUCT IDENTITY by software identity, NOT string equality. An advisory matches when the vulnerable software is the same codebase as an inventory item under any of its names: upstream project ↔ distro package (e.g., advisory says 'OpenSSL', inventory has 'libssl3'; advisory says 'Linux kernel nf_tables', inventory has a Linux kernel), library ↔ package that bundles or ships it, product ↔ module/component shipped with that product. Name collisions do NOT automatically exclude: 'foo' vs 'foo-server' may or may not be the same software — investigate the description; when uncertain whether two names refer to the same codebase, treat it as a MATCH (include). Only exclude on product identity when you are confident the advisory concerns genuinely different software, a different vendor, or hardware/OS the system clearly does not run.

4. COMPARE VERSIONS NUMERICALLY AND CAREFULLY. This is the most error-prone step; redo every comparison explicitly. Rules: (a) compare version segments numerically ('1.10' > '1.9', '2.0.1' < '2.0.10'); (b) epochs dominate ('2:0.9' > '1:5.0'); (c) pre-release suffixes (rc, beta, dev) sort BELOW the release ('1.2rc1' < '1.2'); (d) a version is fixed ONLY if the advisory explicitly marks that version (or the corresponding upstream version) as fixed — a distro-backported version string (e.g., '1.2.3-1.el9+deb4u1') does NOT mean fixed by itself; strip packaging suffixes and compare the upstream version to the affected range. If the installed upstream version falls in the affected range and no explicit fixed entry covers it, it is AFFECTED. (e) When a boundary is ambiguous (inclusive vs exclusive, or unclear whether the range starts at the installed version), err toward INCLUSION — treat it as affected. (f) 'Version unknown/blank' in the inventory should be treated as possibly affected if the product matches and the advisory plausibly covers its era. (g) Only exclude on version when the installed version is STRICTLY below the minimum affected version, or is AT or ABOVE a version the advisory explicitly lists as fixed.

5. CHECK CONSTRAINTS: platform, edition, architecture, or configuration preconditions apply only if the advisory states them AND the inventory clearly violates them; otherwise treat as satisfied.

6. BIAS STRONGLY TOWARD RECALL. Evaluate EVERY advisory in the list — never stop early, never skip advisories requiring multi-step name chaining (advisory → vendor product → upstream project → distro package → inventory item) or careful version arithmetic. Most errors are MISSED APPLICABLE advisories, so: before excluding any advisory, re-verify the product identity against your full inventory index (did you miss an alternate name? a bundled copy? a subsystem of an installed product?) and redo the version comparison numerically. If any doubt remains about product match, version boundary, or constraints, INCLUDE the advisory. Exclude only with clear, specific justification on all three dimensions.

7. OUTPUT — return ONLY a single JSON object, no markdown fences, no prose, no explanation:
{"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]}
The array must contain unique CVE IDs exactly as supplied in the input list, drawn only from the supplied advisories. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}.","feedback":{"error_counts":{"invalid_output":1,"missed_applicable":41,"transport_failure":0,"unrelated_product":22,"version_excluded":9},"metrics":{"coverage":0.9583333333333334,"failure_aware_lower_bound":{"fn":52,"fp":44,"micro_f1":0.35135135135135137,"precision":0.37142857142857144,"recall":0.3333333333333333,"tp":26},"scheduled":24,"valid":23,"valid_answers":{"fn":41,"fp":31,"micro_f1":0.41935483870967744,"precision":0.45614035087719296,"recall":0.3880597014925373,"tp":26}}},"feedback_version":"relational-abstractions-v2","task":"Write an instruction for matching a system inventory to a supplied list of CVE advisories. Input is JSON containing system_profile and advisories. Each advisory supplies its ID, description, and affected information. The answer must be a JSON object whose applicable_cves array contains unique IDs from that supplied list. Return your instruction as a JSON object with one nonempty prompt string of at most 8000 characters.","tier":1}
